parasite

/PARE-uh-syt/ — stress on first syllable, 'site' rhymes with 'knight' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A parasite is an organism that lives on or inside another organism, taking what it needs to survive while harming or giving nothing back to its host.

The tick is a parasite that feeds on the blood of deer.

Worked Example

A lamprey attaches to a salmon, draining its blood meal after meal, leaving the fish weakened and scarred but still alive.

The lamprey lives on and in the salmon without killing it, feeding over time by draining its blood. Parasite is more precise than 'predator' because it names the relationship of living in or on a host and depending on it, not hunting and killing.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pest: A pest is any creature that makes trouble for people — mice in the pantry, aphids on the roses — and the word measures the nuisance it causes, not how it lives. A parasite is defined by its way of living: it feeds on a living host while giving nothing back.

predator: A predator hunts down other animals, kills them, and eats them; the attack ends the encounter then and there. A parasite never wants its host dead — it lives on or in the host's body and keeps drawing food from it, meal after meal, over time.

invader: An invader pushes into a place where it does not belong and takes it over — an army crossing a border, a weed overrunning a garden. The word is about seized territory. A parasite is about feeding: it lives off a host's own body while giving nothing back.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

mutualist: a living thing whose partnership helps both sides

benefactor: one who gives help or benefit to another

Where it sits · how much harm the taking causes — guest → dependent → parasite → infestation

guest vs. parasite: A guest is welcomed and offers friendship in return, far milder than a parasite, which takes from its host while giving nothing back.

dependent vs. parasite: A dependent relies on another for support but is cared for willingly, unlike a parasite, whose reliance actively harms the host it feeds on.

infestation vs. parasite: An infestation is even more severe than a single parasite, describing so many parasites overrunning a host or place that the harm multiplies.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — para-

Prefix — para-: beside, alongside (Greek)

Root — sit-

Root — sit-: food, grain (from Greek 'sitos') (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: 'Para-' means beside and 'sit-' means food, so a parasite is literally one that eats 'beside' another — feeding at its host's table and taking food while giving nothing in return.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: The Greek root sitos ('food, grain') built no other everyday English word; parasite is its only common survivor. In ancient Greece a parasitos was literally a professional dinner guest, someone who earned meals at a rich man's table with flattery instead of work. Biology later borrowed the freeloader's name for any creature that feeds at its host's expense.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Parasite is the precise term for an organism living in or on another organism, depending on it while causing harm. Use it when describing this specific biological relationship. For casual reference to an annoying person or creature, 'pest' or 'freeloader' might work, but parasite is far more exact and scientific.
